newsitem.title: USA: Diverse coalition to fight U.S. campaign reform.
newsitem.headline: Diverse coalition to fight U.S. campaign reform.

text.p: Despite a national scandal over campaign finances, an unusally diverse coalition from civil libertarians to fire fighters on Friday launched a drive to kill off any reform of the system.

Kentucky Sen. Mitch McConnell brought together groups he said represented 15 million people to oppose legislation to reform the campaign system, arguing that pending proposals would violate free political speech rights to donate money to politicians or run ads for them.
At a news conference in a Senate room, McConnell lined up behind him representatives from various organisations that often are on different sides of issues.

They included civil libertarians, broadcasters, teachers, Christian activists, firearms proponents, letter carriers, fire fighters, real estate agents, direct mail marketers and anti-abortion activists.
Their common enemy was bipartisan legislation sponsored in the Senate by Republican John McCain of Arizona and Democrat Russ Feingold of Wisconsin and by a bipartisan group in the House.

That legislation has not gathered much steam in the Republican-led Congress despite daily doses of stories about campaign finance abuses that has snarled President Bill Clinton and Democrats in controversy.
The campaign reform bill would put curbs on spending and donations to federal campaigns but McConnell and his coaliton of backers saw a threat to free speech in the legislation.
"McCain-Feingold is to democracy what the Clinton health care plan was to medicine," McConnell said about Clinton's ill-fated proposal for national health insurance.

He also opposed a pending measure in the Senate to overcome Supreme Court objections to campaign spending limits. The legislation, to be voted on Tuesday, would, if approved by two-thirds of the Senate and House and three-fourths of the states, add an amendment to the Constitution to let Congress limit spending and donations.
McConnell predicted the constitutional amendment plan would be defeated on Tuesday and also said Congress would not pass the McCain-Feingold plan this year.
But he gathered the coalition as a pre-emptive strike if there is a public outcry later for reform when House and Senate hearings into campaign abuses start this spring.
"The campaign finance debate is far from over," said McConnell. "As you know it will be a huge story later because of violations of existing law last year," he said.

McConnell argued that the constitutional amendment plan and separate McCain-Feingold bill would restrict political speech and he noted the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) says it would make the media "fair game for regulation."
Laura Murphy, director of the ACLU Washington office, said "we have long opposed government restraints on when, with whom and how to engage in political speech."
Her organisation supports taxpayer-paid campaign financing.

Organisations lining up to oppose pending legislation were the ACLU, National Right to Life Committee, National Education Association, the Christian Coalition, National Rifle Association, Direct Marketing Association, National Association of Broadcasters, National Association of Realtors, National Rural Letter Carriers Association, National Association of Letter Carriers and the International Association of Fire Fighters.
